165	V: about 40 (whole body); about 4 to 5 (single organ) |U: times the effective sensitivity |R: The factor of about 40 is a design estimate published in 2018 before the scanner was finished. The measured sensitivity of the finished scanner is 174 kcps/MBq (NEMA NU 2-2018 test).
166	SRC: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pmc&id=5750522 ; https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pmc&id=8729871
167	N: Draft confirmed with a caveat. Source wording (Cherry et al., J Nucl Med 2018): "by increasing the geometric coverage to encompass the entire body, sensitivity can be increased by a factor of about 40 for total-body imaging or a factor of about 4 to 5 for imaging a single organ such as the brain or heart". Present it as "about 40 times" or "up to about 40 times" for whole-body scans and say it is a calculated figure; do not say "40 times better pictures". Abstracts only were read.
168	
169	### totalbody-fast-low-dose | Draft claim 8: total-body PET, speed and dose | unverified
170	S: The extra sensitivity can be spent in different ways: the first human studies showed usable whole-body pictures from scans of about 1 minute or less, or with as little as 25 MBq of tracer in the body, a small fraction of the usual 185 to 370 MBq injection.
171	V: about 1 minute or less; 25 MBq or less |U:  |R: Initial case studies (2019), not routine practice. A 2021 patient study on a 106 cm scanner matched a 16-minute standard scan in under 2 minutes.
172	SRC: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pmc&id=6424228 ; https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=TITLE%3A%22head-to-head%20intra-individual%20comparison%20of%20the%20Biograph%20Vision%20Quadra%22&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=3
173	N: Draft confirmed. Source wording (Badawi et al. 2019): "the sensitivity gain can be used to acquire diagnostic PET images with very small amounts of activity in the field of view (25 MBq, 0.7 mCi or less), with very short acquisition times (about 1 min or less) or at later time points". The authors call this "initial evidence". Arithmetic (calc.js): 25 MBq x 0.019 = 0.475 mSv from the tracer, and 370 / 25 = 14.8, so 25 MBq is between about one seventh and one fifteenth of the usual 185 to 370 MBq; the abstract says "activity in the field of view", which is not necessarily the injected amount, so the statement says "in the body" and "a small fraction". The same scanner can also film the tracer moving through the whole body with frames as short as 1 second.
174	
175	### tracer-ga68-dotatate | Draft claim 9: other tracers (Ga-68 DOTATATE) | unverified
176	S: Gallium-68 DOTATATE (half-life 68 minutes) sticks to somatostatin receptors and is used to find neuroendocrine tumors.
177	V: 67.71 |U: minutes (half-life of gallium-68) |R: Labels round to 68 min. Gallium-68 comes from a germanium-68 generator (half-life 270.93 days), so no cyclotron is needed on site.
178	SRC: https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/b2b3be70-17d8-4093-896c-f1c54a2cf242.xml ; https://nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=all
179	N: Confirmed against the NETSPOT label: "indicated for use with positron emission tomography (PET) for localization of somatostatin receptor positive neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) in adult and pediatric patients"; label states initial US approval 2016. Half-life from IAEA nuclear data (4062.6 s).
180	
181	### tracer-psma | Draft claim 9: other tracers (PSMA agents) | unverified
182	S: PSMA tracers, made with either gallium-68 (half-life 68 minutes) or fluorine-18 (half-life 110 minutes), stick to a protein on prostate cancer cells and are used to find prostate cancer that has spread or come back.
183	V: Ga-68 gozetotide (PSMA-11): 67.71 min; F-18 piflufolastat (DCFPyL): 109.77 min |U: minutes (half-life) |R: US labels give initial approval years of 2020 for gallium Ga 68 gozetotide (PSMA-11) and 2021 for piflufolastat F 18 (Pylarify).
184	SRC: https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/8683b06e-4901-4526-89ad-23a8fe2d1331.xml ; https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/a00e5cbc-4fd5-4280-82ec-cd3498df4553.xml ; https://nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=all
185	N: Confirmed against the LOCAMETZ and PYLARIFY labels: PET "of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positive lesions in men with prostate cancer" with suspected metastasis before first treatment or suspected recurrence based on a rising PSA. PSMA is prostate-specific membrane antigen. Avoid "first PSMA tracer" claims on the site; the FDA announcement of the 2020 approval could not be opened.
186	
187	### tracer-florbetapir | Draft claim 9: other tracers (F-18 florbetapir) | unverified
188	S: Fluorine-18 florbetapir (half-life 110 minutes) sticks to amyloid plaques in the brain and is used when doctors are investigating Alzheimer's disease and other causes of memory loss.
189	V: 109.77 |U: minutes (half-life of fluorine-18) |R: Other amyloid tracers with the same isotope exist (florbetaben, flutemetamol); they were not checked in this batch.
190	SRC: https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/bb5a5043-0f51-11df-8a39-0800200c9a66.xml ; https://nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=all
191	N: Confirmed against the AMYVID label: PET "of the brain to estimate amyloid beta neuritic plaque density in adults with cognitive impairment" for evaluation of Alzheimer's disease and other causes of cognitive decline, and for selecting patients for amyloid-directed therapy; label states initial US approval 2012. A positive scan shows plaques; it does not by itself diagnose Alzheimer's disease.
192	
193	### tracer-rb82 | Draft claim 9: other tracers (Rb-82) | unverified
194	S: Rubidium-82 has a half-life of only 75 seconds, is drawn fresh from a generator next to the scanner, and is used to map blood flow to the heart muscle at rest and under stress.
195	V: 75.45 |U: seconds (half-life of rubidium-82; 1.2575 minutes) |R: Label rounds to 75 seconds. The generator holds strontium-82 (half-life about 25 days).
196	SRC: https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/ee95aa18-9f2f-40eb-9b4c-583bea6f36bf.xml ; https://nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=all
197	N: Confirmed against the CardioGen-82 label: PET "of the myocardium under rest or pharmacologic stress conditions to evaluate regional myocardial perfusion in adult patients with suspected or existing coronary artery disease"; label states initial US approval 1989. After 10 minutes only 0.404% of the rubidium-82 is left (calc.js).
198	
199	### tracer-n13-ammonia | Draft claim 9: other tracers (N-13 ammonia) | unverified
200	S: Nitrogen-13 ammonia has a half-life of about 10 minutes, so it must be made in a cyclotron close to the scanner, and it is also used to map blood flow to the heart muscle.
201	V: 9.965 |U: minutes (half-life of nitrogen-13) |R: Label rounds to 9.96 minutes.
202	SRC: https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/b1559f8a-1fc8-4a9e-b4f4-5e2efcb1f12c.xml ; https://nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=all
203	N: Confirmed against an Ammonia N 13 Injection label: "diagnostic PET imaging of the myocardium under rest or pharmacologic stress conditions to evaluate myocardial perfusion in patients with suspected or existing coronary artery disease". The label read prints "Initial U.S. Approval: 2007"; do not use this as the date ammonia PET began, since the tracer was in research use decades earlier. "Close to the scanner" is this project's inference from the 10-minute half-life (half is gone every 10 minutes: 1.54% left after an hour, calc.js).
204	
205	### scan-painless | Draft claim 10: comfort | unverified
206	S: The scan itself does not hurt; the only pain is the brief sting of the needle for the injection, and the hardest part for most people is lying still.
207	V: painless apart from the injection |U:  |R: 
208	SRC: https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003827.htm ; https://www.radiologyinfo.org/en/info/pet ; https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/tests-and-scans/pet-ct-scan
209	N: Draft confirmed. MedlinePlus: "A PET scan causes no pain" and "You may feel a sharp sting when the needle with the tracer is placed into your vein". RadiologyInfo: "Except for intravenous injections, most nuclear medicine procedures are painless." Cancer Research UK: "The scan is painless but can be uncomfortable because you have to stay still." Rare problems mentioned by these sources: tracer leaking outside the vein, and rare allergic reactions. People who fear closed spaces can be given a calming medicine.
210	
211	### precaution-pregnancy | Draft claim 10: pregnancy | unverified
212	S: Patients are asked to tell the staff if they are or might be pregnant, because the tracer crosses the placenta and the unborn baby would receive some radiation, so the scan is done in pregnancy only when doctors judge that the benefit outweighs that risk.
213	V: benefit weighed against risk case by case |U:  |R: Cancer Research UK: "Pregnant women should only have the scan in an emergency." EANM: "a clinical decision is necessary in which the benefits are weighed against the possible harm".
214	SRC: https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/5d05df4a-463e-4e66-9387-f3a842e20cd0.xml ; https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4315529/fullTextXML ; https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/tests-and-scans/pet-ct-scan ; https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003827.htm ; https://www.radiologyinfo.org/en/info/pet
215	N: FDA label: published reports "describe Fludeoxyglucose F 18 Injection crossing the placenta with uptake by the fetus"; "All radiopharmaceuticals have the potential to cause fetal harm depending on the fetal stage of development and the magnitude of the radiation dose"; published studies "have not identified a risk of drug-associated major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes". The CT part adds further dose to the baby. Keep the wording neutral: pregnancy is a reason for caution, not an absolute ban.
216	
217	### precaution-breastfeeding | Draft claim 10: breastfeeding | unverified
218	S: Breastfeeding mothers get specific instructions, which differ between countries: the United States drug label says to pump and discard milk and avoid close contact with the baby for 9 hours after the injection, while European guidance says breastfeeding need not stop but close contact should be limited for 12 hours.
219	V: 9 (US FDA label); 12 (European guideline, contact only) |U: hours |R: NHS: "not breastfeeding for a few hours afterwards". RadiologyInfo: pump milk ahead of time to use until the tracer is gone.
220	SRC: https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/5d05df4a-463e-4e66-9387-f3a842e20cd0.xml ; https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4315529/fullTextXML ; https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/pet-scan/ ; https://www.radiologyinfo.org/en/info/pet
221	N: FDA label: "advise a lactating woman to pump and discard breastmilk and avoid close (breast) contact with the infant for at least 9 hours". EANM 2015: "The ICRP does not recommend interruption of breastfeeding after FDG administration since little FDG is excreted in the milk ... it is suggested that contact between mother and child be limited for 12 h". The reason in both cases is mainly radiation from the mother's body (the breast itself takes up FDG), not the milk. A US Nuclear Regulatory Commission guide (Regulatory Guide 8.39 Rev. 1) also gives interruption times but could not be opened. 1	### prep-fasting | Draft claim 1: preparation (fasting) | unverified
2	S: Before an FDG PET/CT scan for cancer, patients are asked not to eat or drink anything except plain water for at least 4 to 6 hours.
3	V: at least 4 (European guideline); 4 to 6 (US guideline and FDA drug label) |U: hours |R: European guideline (EANM 2015): at least 4 h before injection. US guideline (SNM 2006): at least 4 to 6 h. FDA label: 4 to 6 h. Many hospitals simply say 6 h (NHS, UCSF).
4	SRC: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4315529/fullTextXML ; https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/jnumed/47/5/885.full.pdf ; https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/5d05df4a-463e-4e66-9387-f3a842e20cd0.xml ; https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/pet-scan/ ; https://radiology.ucsf.edu/patient-care/prepare/pet-ct
5	N: Draft confirmed. Drinking water is encouraged, not just allowed (EANM suggests about 1 L in the 2 h before injection). The fasting rule applies to cancer and brain scans; for the heart-viability scan the FDA label instead describes giving glucose (50 to 75 g) before injection, and scans for heart inflammation or infection may need a longer fast or a low-carbohydrate diet. Do not present 4 to 6 hours as a rule for every FDG scan.
6	
7	### prep-blood-glucose | Draft claim 1: preparation (blood glucose) | unverified
8	S: Staff check the blood sugar before the injection, and under European guidance the scan goes ahead if it is below 11 mmol/L (about 200 mg/dL).
9	V: 11 (about 200 mg/dL) |U: mmol/L |R: EANM 2015: below 11 mmol/L (about 200 mg/dL) for clinical scans; 7 to 8.3 mmol/L (126 to 150 mg/dL) as the upper limit in research studies. SNM 2006: most institutions reschedule above 150 to 200 mg/dL.
10	SRC: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4315529/fullTextXML ; https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/jnumed/47/5/885.full.pdf ; https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/5d05df4a-463e-4e66-9387-f3a842e20cd0.xml
11	N: Draft confirmed. Unit check (calc.js): 11 mmol/L = 198 mg/dL and 200 mg/dL = 11.1 mmol/L, so "about 200 mg/dL" is a rounding. The reason: high blood sugar and insulin push FDG into muscle and reduce tumor uptake. EANM also says the level should not be too low (not below 4 mmol/L, about 70 mg/dL). Thresholds differ between hospitals, so keep the word "about" or name the guideline.
12	
13	### prep-exercise | Draft claim 1: preparation (exercise) | unverified
14	S: Patients are asked to avoid strenuous exercise for at least 6 hours, and preferably 24 hours, before the scan, because working muscles take up the tracer.
15	V: at least 6, preferably 24 |U: hours |R: EANM 2015: at least 6 h, preferably 24 h. NHS: up to 24 hours. Cancer Research UK: 24 hours.
16	SRC: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4315529/fullTextXML ; https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/pet-scan/ ; https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/tests-and-scans/pet-ct-scan
17	N: Draft said "about 24 hours"; the guideline wording is "at least 6 h ... and preferably for 24 h". Either form is safe if 24 hours is called the usual advice rather than a strict rule.
18	
19	### uptake-time | Draft claim 2: uptake time | unverified
20	S: After the injection the patient waits about 60 minutes before the scan starts, so that the tracer can spread through the body and collect in the tissues that use the most sugar.
21	V: 60 |U: minutes |R: EANM 2015: 60 min recommended, acceptable range 55 to 75 min. SNM 2006: images typically acquired more than 45 min after injection. FDA label: static images 30 to 100 min after injection. Brain-only scans can start earlier (30 to 50 min).
22	SRC: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4315529/fullTextXML ; https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/jnumed/47/5/885.full.pdf ; https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/5d05df4a-463e-4e66-9387-f3a842e20cd0.xml ; https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/tests-and-scans/pet-ct-scan ; https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/pet-scan/
23	N: Draft confirmed (60 min, 55 to 75 min). The 55 to 75 minute window comes from the European guideline and exists to keep uptake measurements (SUV) comparable between scans; it is not a safety limit. For a repeat scan of the same patient the guideline asks for the same waiting time to within 10 minutes.
24	
25	### uptake-rest | Draft claim 2: what the patient does during uptake | unverified
26	S: During the wait the patient sits or lies still in a warm, quiet room and is asked not to talk, because moving, talking and feeling cold all send tracer to muscle or brown fat instead of where the doctors want to look.
27	V: seated or lying down, silent, kept warm |U:  |R: Same advice in European and US guidelines; for brain scans the room is also dimly lit.
28	SRC: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4315529/fullTextXML ; https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/jnumed/47/5/885.full.pdf ; https://www.radiologyinfo.org/en/info/pet
29	N: Added detail, not in the draft. EANM: "the patient should remain seated or recumbent and silent" and "should be kept warm starting 30 to 60 min before the injection" to limit uptake in brown fat. Patients may use the toilet, and are asked to empty the bladder just before the scan.
30	
31	### scan-ct-time | Draft claim 3: CT pass | unverified
32	S: The CT pass comes first and takes less than two minutes.
33	V: less than 2 |U: minutes |R: Depends on scanner and scan length; the X-ray beam itself is usually on for well under a minute on a modern multi-slice CT, but the only figure found in a patient-facing professional source is "less than two minutes".
34	SRC: https://www.radiologyinfo.org/en/info/pet
35	N: Draft said "under a minute". CORRECTED to "less than two minutes", the wording of RadiologyInfo.org (RSNA and ACR): "The CT scan takes less than two minutes." No authoritative source was found that states "under a minute" for the whole CT step, so the safer figure is used.
36	
37	### scan-pet-time | Draft claim 3: PET pass | unverified
38	S: The PET pass takes longer, usually about 15 to 30 minutes on a standard scanner, and the patient has to lie still for all of it.
39	V: 15 to 30 |U: minutes |R: SNM guideline 2006: 15 to 45 min for skull to mid-thigh. RadiologyInfo: PET scan 20 to 30 min, total scanning about 30 min.
